topic: Peptides your body makes: gastrin, the stomach's acid switch. Gastrin is a peptide hormone made by G cells of the gastric antrum and duodenum (StatPearls 'Physiology, Gastrin' 2023); released by gastric distension, peptides/amino acids, vagal/GRP stimulation and raised stomach pH; acts on parietal cell CCK-B receptors and makes ECL cells release histamine, which further drives acid (StatPearls 2023; Duan, Rico & Merchant, Function 2021); acid (pH<3) makes antral D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin (Duan 2021); Edkins named gastrin in 1905, largely dismissed; Gregory & Tracy (Gut 1964) isolated two 17-amino-acid gastrins (heptadecapeptides), the first GI peptide with full structure solved

Peptides your body makes

Your stomach has its own acid switch.

Its name: gastrin.

Meet gastrin

A peptide hormone

Made by G cells in the lower stomach and the first part of the gut.

What switches it ON
1

Food stretches the stomach

2

Protein pieces arrive

3

The vagus nerve sends a signal

What it does

Gastrin → parietal cells

"Make acid."

Plus a helper

It also triggers histamine, which adds more acid.

What switches it OFF

When acid gets strong, D cells release somatostatin.

Gastrin stops.

How we found it

1905

John Edkins named it gastrin. Few believed him.

1964

Gregory and Tracy isolated it: 17 amino acids long.

Save this for your physiology exam.
